claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy is a non-equilibrium, metastable solid solution.
The initial alloy has a uniform elemental distribution.
Prolonged aging above 600°C in a corrosive environment activates a diffusion-controlled transformation in the alloy.
The transformation produces localized Mg-enriched intermetallic precipitates.
The Mg-enriched intermetallic precipitates preferentially nucleate and grow at grain boundaries.
Mg diffuses and segregates to grain boundaries during high-temperature exposure.
Grain-boundary segregation of Mg facilitates intermetallic-phase nucleation and growth.
The intermetallic precipitates alter the local chemical environment.
The intermetallic precipitates disrupt the continuity of the protective oxide scale.
Disruption of the protective oxide scale modifies oxidation kinetics.
The precipitate-mediated microstructural evolution modifies corrosion resistance and passivation behavior relative to the initial state.
Aged samples will contain discrete grain-boundary Mg-enriched intermetallic precipitates relative to the initially homogeneous state.
The precipitate evolution will correlate with measurable changes in oxide-scale formation.
Temperatures at or above 600°C and aggressive salt-spray-type exposure define the service regime in which the proposed mechanism is expected to operate.
The proposed effects may not be observable under milder temperature or corrosion conditions.
Processing that enhances grain-boundary segregation will produce behavior measurably different from processing that minimizes segregation after aging near 650°C.
